title: Relationship-Specificity, Incomplete Contracts, and the Pattern of Trade
research_question: Does a country's ability to enforce written contracts shape its comparative advantage in international trade? Specifically, do countries with stronger contract enforcement specialize in exporting goods whose production relies more heavily on intermediate inputs requiring relationship-specific investments?
data_description: The unit of observation is a country-industry pair, with industries classified according to the BEA's 1997 Input-Output system (222 industries total, 182 manufacturing). Bilateral trade flows for 1997 (exports from each country to the rest of the world) come from Feenstra's World Trade Flows database, originally in 4-digit SITC and reclassified to I-O industries. Production data are from UNIDO. Factor endowments (physical capital per worker, ratio of high-school completers) for 1992 are from Antweiler and Trefler; factor intensities from Bartelsman and Gray. Judicial quality is measured primarily by Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi's 1997-1998 'rule of law' index, with robustness measures from Gwartney-Lawson and World Bank Doing Business. Contract intensity of each industry is constructed from the 1997 U.S. I-O Use Table combined with Rauch's (1999) classification of inputs as sold on organized exchanges, reference priced, or neither. Sample covers up to 146 countries. Historical data from 1963 are also used.
institutional_context: The setting is global trade in 1997, where countries differ markedly in the quality of their judicial systems and ability to enforce written contracts. When suppliers must make customized, relationship-specific investments to produce intermediate inputs for downstream producers, weak contract enforcement creates hold-up risk and leads to underinvestment ex ante. This friction varies systematically across goods: products like petroleum, flour, or basic metals rely on standardized inputs traded on thick markets, while automobiles, aircraft, and electronics depend heavily on customized components with few alternative buyers or sellers. Countries also differ in legal traditions—British common law, French civil law, German civil law, Scandinavian, and Socialist origins—which historically shape judicial efficiency. These cross-country institutional differences, combined with cross-industry differences in reliance on relationship-specific inputs, create the variation needed to assess whether contracting institutions act as a source of comparative advantage alongside traditional factor endowments.
